finding.claim: Caller identity is taken from the client-supplied X-Session-User-Verified header with no signature, token, or trusted-proxy check, so any client can impersonate any user and delete or rename files they hold an ID for.
finding.source: X-Session-User-Verified request header (views.py:11, read via request.headers.get in before_request)
finding.sink: ensure_allowed in delete_file (views.py:17, guarding del STORE[fid] at views.py:18) and is_allowed in rename_file (views.py:25, guarding f["name"] assignment at views.py:27)

trace.note: before_request load_user registers for every request
g.user set directly from the unverified request header
is_allowed looks up grants by the spoofed g.user key
abort(403) only when the spoofed identity lacks the grant
deletion proceeds for an impersonated, authorized identity

finding.guards_checked: ensure_allowed/is_allowed enforce grants correctly but against the spoofed identity; no signature, session, or token verification exists; no origin check on the header; absent header yields None which is denied. Exploitable only if the app is reachable without a proxy that strips and rewrites this header; deployment config not present in repo. Weakens authentication: flag for Security review.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) and is_allowed (acl.py:4-5) enforce grants, but only for whatever identity g.user holds; g.user is set straight from the request header at views.py:11, and the checks are tested at views.py:17 (bare call, abort(403) on failure) and views.py:25 (boolean tested). No signature, session, or trusted-proxy check exists anywhere in views.py or acl.py.
verdict.reason: views.py:11 takes the caller identity from the client-supplied X-Session-User-Verified header, and nothing in the repo verifies it, so any client that sends the header as a granted user passes ensure_allowed at views.py:17 and reaches del STORE[fid] at views.py:18 (or is_allowed at views.py:25 and the rename at views.py:27). The only caveat is deployment: if a reverse proxy strips and rewrites this header in front of the app, the attack is blocked, but that config is not in the repo, so the flaw is confirmed at code level and should be flagged for Security review.

finding.claim: Unknown file IDs raise an unhandled KeyError before any authorization check, returning 500, while existing-but-forbidden IDs return 403, so an unauthenticated caller can enumerate which file IDs exist.
finding.source: fid URL path segment (views.py:14-15 for delete, views.py:22-23 for rename), attacker-controlled
finding.sink: STORE[fid] lookup before ensure_allowed/is_allowed (views.py:16 and views.py:24)

trace.note: delete_file receives attacker-controlled fid from the route
STORE[fid] raises KeyError for an unknown ID, before any ACL check
403 path only reached for IDs that exist

finding.guards_checked: 403 path works for existing IDs; no try/except or 404 for missing IDs; no auth gate before the lookup. Severity low, depends on ID guessability.

verdict.guard_found: none. views.py:16 and views.py:24 index STORE[fid] before any check. The only auth-related code is the before_request at views.py:9-11, which just copies a header into g.user and does not reject anything. acl.py:4-10 (is_allowed/ensure_allowed) runs only after the lookup, and no error handler in views.py converts KeyError to 404.
verdict.reason: An anonymous caller (no X-Session-User-Verified header, so g.user is None, and is_allowed returns False at acl.py:5) hitting an unknown fid gets an unhandled KeyError at views.py:16 or views.py:24 (500), while an existing fid gets abort(403) from acl.py:10, so the status code distinguishes existing from non-existing IDs. The impact is a low-severity ID-existence oracle, not a data access bypass.

finding.claim: The grant membership check is a substring match when a grant value is a string rather than a list, so an action such as "write" is granted by a value like "rewrite" that was never intended.
finding.source: grants data structure supplied by resource creation/storage (not validated in this repo); the value at grants[user]
finding.sink: action in resource.get("grants", {}).get(user, []) at acl.py:5, which gates delete (views.py:17) and rename (views.py:25)

trace.note: Python 'in' performs substring match if grants[user] is a str, exact match if a list

finding.guards_checked: Membership test is exact when grants are lists (safe); no type check on grant values in this code. Conditional on how grants are populated, which is not visible in the repo. Severity low.

verdict.guard_found: none. ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) calls is_allowed and aborts on False, so it is not bypassed, but is_allowed (acl.py:5) has no type check on the grant value. The rename path (views.py:25) uses is_allowed directly with "write", as the candidate's sink says it should.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: acl.py:5 uses Python `in`, which is a substring match when the value is a str, and views.py:17 and views.py:25 pass "delete" and "write" into it. Whether that is reachable depends on how grants are stored, and the repo has no resource-creation or grant-writing code (STORE at views.py:6 is an empty dict), so I cannot tell if any grant value is ever a string. The candidate's own "conditional" note and "low" severity are consistent with that.

finding.claim: Rename stores request.json["name"] without type or length validation, so non-string or oversized values are persisted and a missing body or key causes a 500.
finding.source: JSON request body field "name" (views.py:27), attacker-controlled, only reachable after the write check passes
finding.sink: f["name"] assignment in rename_file (views.py:27), persisting into the shared STORE

trace.note: is_allowed(g.user, f, "write") gate passes for an authorized caller
request.json["name"] is stored with no type, length, or content validation; request.json None or missing key raises

finding.guards_checked: Write authorization check runs first, so only authorized callers reach this. No rendering of the stored name appears in this code; if another component renders it unescaped it becomes a stored XSS or injection sink. Severity low, pending the rest of the system.

verdict.guard_found: views.py:25 `if not is_allowed(g.user, f, "write")` is a bool check that returns 403 before the store at views.py:27; acl.py:4-5 `is_allowed` returns `action in resource.get("grants", {}).get(user, [])`. Nothing validates the type or length of `request.json["name"]`.
verdict.reason: The trace lines match the code (views.py:25 gate, views.py:27 unvalidated store), but the only caller who can reach the store is one already granted "write" (acl.py:5, views.py:25), and that grant already lets them set `name` to any string. The remaining effects (a self-inflicted 500 on a missing key, and non-string values stored in STORE) give no privilege beyond write, and no code in this repo renders the stored name, so the claimed XSS/injection sink is unsupported here and is at most a robustness issue.
